title: dev-onboard-map map.json: the learned model of one codebase, every claim cited
description: Written by dev-onboard-map to <evid_root>/onboard/<project>/map.json, read by qa-onboard-quiz (the examiner answers from THIS file and nothing else), dev-onboard-teach, the staleness check and the brain write-back. It is the onboarding loop's product: a codebase described as areas plus atomic claims, where every claim says what it rests on. A claim about how the code behaves cites file and line. A claim about why it is that way cites the record (a commit, a pull request, a decision doc) or says it is an inference. The quiz grades the map, not the agent that wrote it, so a map that cannot answer a question is a map bug with an area and a class. See docs/onboarding-loop.md.

project.description: The project name, the same one qa-kb stamps on brain rows.

commit.description: The full commit SHA of the code this map describes. The staleness check diffs from here, so a map with no real commit is stale everywhere.

summary.description: What this system is, in two or three plain sentences a senior engineer would say out loud: the general name for the thing, then what this codebase uses it for.

areas.description: The units the codebase splits into. An area is the grain of fan-out, of quiz scoring and of relearning. Seeded from survey.json and corrected by the how cards.

id.description: Stable short id, lowercase, used by claims, questions and router work items.

paths.description: Path prefixes this area covers. The staleness check maps changed files to areas through these.

purpose.description: One sentence: the job this area does for the system.

depends_on.description: Area ids this area calls into.

claims.description: Atomic facts. One claim says one thing and can be checked on its own.

id.description: Stable id, e.g. invoices.c3. The examiner names claim ids in its answers; the grader checks they exist.

kind.description: what = what a thing is. how = a runtime flow or mechanism. where = where something lives. owner = which module owns a piece of state or a decision. why = the reason it is built this way. rule = where new code of a given kind belongs (the architect lens). gotcha = a trap a newcomer would hit. command = how to build, test, run or lint.

text.description: The claim in one or two plain sentences. No hedging words; confidence carries the hedge.

cites.description: What the claim rests on. Code cites carry path and lines; record cites carry ref. Empty only for a why claim marked source=inference.

symbol.description: A name that must appear in the cited lines. The grader checks it, which catches a cite that drifted.

ref.description: A record pointer for a why claim: commit:<sha>, pr:<number>, doc:<path>.

evidence.description: How far the claim was proven. said = asserted only (never enough for a non-why claim). pointed = a real file and line. walked = the flow was traced step by step and the bad case does not reach. ran = a command or test that calls the real code showed it.

confidence.description: Mainly for why claims. certain = the record says so in the authors' words. likely = a strong inference. guessing = filling a gap. A why claim that is an inference may not be certain.

verified_round.description: The quiz round in which a question that leaned on this claim was answered correctly. The write-back promotes only verified claims.

commands.description: build / test / lint / run as the repo itself declares them (from survey.json), each a string. Copied, never invented.

open_questions.description: What the code and the record do not answer. Saying so is a finding, not a failure.
